title: Mean and Variance of a Continuous Variable
short: E[X] = ∫ x f(x) dx and E[g(X)] = ∫ g(x) f(x) dx, and the variance shortcut still holds.
trouble: Students integrate f(x) alone and get 1, forgetting the factor x.

blocks.html: For a discrete variable the mean is $\sum x\,P(X = x)$. For a density the sum becomes an integral, and every rule from the variance rules carries over unchanged.

Cut the line into thin slices of width $\Delta x$. The slice at $x$ has probability about $f(x)\,\Delta x$, so the discrete formula gives $\sum x\,f(x)\,\Delta x$, a Riemann sum that tends to $\int x\,f(x)\,dx$. Geometrically, $E[X]$ is the balance point of the region under the density, the place where a ruler shaped like the graph would balance on a finger. The same slicing gives $E[g(X)]$, and the algebra behind the variance shortcut only used linearity, which integrals have too.

blocks.name: prob-density
blocks.cap: The density 2x on 0 to 1, with its balance point at two thirds and its median a little higher.

blocks.title: The uniform distribution
blocks.q: $X$ is uniform on $[a, b]$. Find $E[X]$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)$.
steps: $f = \frac{1}{b - a}$ on $[a, b]$. $$E[X] = \int_{a}^{b} \frac{x}{b - a}\,dx = \frac{b^{2} - a^{2}}{2(b - a)} = \frac{a + b}{2}$$ the midpoint.

blocks.title: A function of X
steps: Compare $\frac{1}{E[X]} = \frac{3}{2}$: as in the discrete case, $E[g(X)] \ne g(E[X])$.

blocks.html: Any function works the same way. Powers give the moments $E[X^{3}] = \int x^{3}f(x)\,dx$, and so on. A squared distance from a number $c$ can be expanded first, $$E[(X - c)^{2}] = E[X^{2}] - 2cE[X] + c^{2}$$ so two integrals you may already have do the work. And for a curved function such as $e^{x}$, expect the average of the function to exceed the function of the average: for $X$ uniform on $[0, 1]$, $E[e^{X}] = e - 1 \approx 1.72$ while $e^{E[X]} = e^{1/2} \approx 1.65$.

Integrating the density alone, $\int f(x)\,dx$, and reporting the result as the mean. That integral is always 1. Check: the mean must lie inside the range of $X$, and you need the factor $x$ (or $g(x)$) inside the integral.
